threat_assessment:
They look at your command zone, count to nine, and file you under durdle. Let them keep the read. The Ur-Dragon arrives on turn nine on average and never once by turn six, so stop building turns around him and spend the head start their patience is giving you.

Do not read that nine as a schedule. The simulation does not model Urza's Incubator, Herald's Horn or Dragonspeaker Shaman, so it is a ceiling, not a clock — and a reducer is in hand by turn six only 33.2% of the time, so when one shows up, cast the discounted Dragon rather than saving the discount for the commander.

Play the first four turns as fixing, not as menace. You have 1.463 bodies on the battlefield by turn six, which is not a board anybody breaks a sweeper for — so let the token player be the wide one and take the free pass (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection).

Take the land drop every single time. It holds at 88.3% on turn three, then falls to 60.3% on five and 49.7% on six, so on the two turns your plan has to start deploying you miss a land as often as you hit one. Keep the two-lander only when there is a rock in it, and take fixing over utility in every choice you are offered.

Do not count Mox Jasper as mana in an opening hand. It only taps while you control a Dragon, so it is a blank until the board arrives.

Now the tells — and you own the timing on every one of them.

Aggravated Assault is the loudest card in the deck and the one you cannot replace. All three of your two-card infinites route through it, and of your seven tutors only Enlightened Tutor can find an enchantment at all. Put it on the battlefield the turn it wins, never on the turn the mana happened to be spare.

Miirym buys removal almost as fast, because everyone at the table has watched her double someone's board (stack 002). Sneak Attack reads as a combo card the instant it resolves (stack 005). Tiamat announces five specific Dragons as she enters. Dragon Tempest is invisible until you go wide, and then it is the first thing they answer (stack 001).

Enlightened Tutor, Worldly Tutor and Teferi's Protection are your three Game Changers. The turn one of them resolves, assume removal is being held for your combat step and move your window a turn earlier.

Count real mana before you declare attackers, because five of your sources lie to you at exactly the wrong moment. Haven of the Spirit Dragon, Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon, Unclaimed Territory, Rivaz of the Claw and an attacking Klauth all make mana you may spend only on casting spells — and Assault's {3}{R}{R} is an activated ability. Pay it from lands, rocks and Treasures, and total it in your precombat main phase rather than after you have tapped out.

Turn six gives you 4.937 mana on average. That is one Assault activation and nothing else, so if you want the first extra combat on curve, bank a Treasure before you get there.

Do not wait for the loop. Assault plus a mana dragon assembles in 6.4% of games and 3.6% by turn six at a mean of turn five and a half — treat it as your ceiling and play toward the other number, because a Dragon payoff is in hand in 73.1% of games and 62.2% by turn six. Build toward Tempest and a board; take the loop when it walks in.

Take the archenemy seat on exactly two boards, and choose both moments yourself.

The first is Assault live with a Dragon connecting. Go, and buy every combat you can pay for. Old Gnawbone nets two Treasures a cycle and kills a 40-life opponent on combat six and the next on combat twelve without your five lands ever tapping (stack 006); Savage Ventmaw pays its own reactivation with a mana to spare (stack 003). Count the combats first and check nothing on their board eats the Dragon halfway through.

The second is a damage sweeper coming while Wrathful Red Dragon is on the battlefield. Say the arithmetic out loud before their turn: three of your Dragons taking damage sends 39 at one player, and two Dragons sends only 26 (stack 004). Naming a number that kills one specific seat usually keeps the wrath in their hand, which most nights is worth more to you than the kill.

Cavern-Hoard Dragon is listed as a third infinite with Assault and nothing has signed it — its Treasures count the defending player's artifacts, so it needs a stack scenario before you build a turn on it. Attack, bank the Treasures, treat the loop as a bonus.

Then go back to being the ramp deck with the expensive commander. You own the longest game at this table (strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock), and nothing they are pointing removal at is the thing that actually wins it.
matchups:
VS SWEEPER CONTROL. They are holding the wrath for your Dragon wave, so make holding it the mistake. Get Wrathful Red Dragon down before you go wide, and any damage-based sweeper becomes a trap they walk into (stack 004). Respect the edge of that: destroy-all and exile-all wraths feed him nothing.

Deploy in waves and buy resilience instead of restraint — against a control seat, holding back is the loss, because the time you spend waiting is the exact resource they are collecting (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math). At 1.463 bodies by turn six you are barely handing them a target anyway.

Rebuild cheaper than they can answer. Aggravated Assault, Sneak Attack, Dragon Tempest, Garruk's Uprising and Temur Ascendancy all sit under a creature wrath untouched, and Atsushi dies forward into three Treasures that legally pay Assault's activation. Spend Counterspell, Swan Song and Dovin's Veto on the sweeper, not on the first scary creature you see.

Hellkite Courser is your best post-wrath turn. He is the only card in the deck that puts The Ur-Dragon onto the battlefield from the command zone, hasted for one attack and one eminence draw; Sneak Attack cannot reach that zone (stack 005).

Price your free spells honestly. Deflecting Swat and Flawless Maneuver cost nothing only while you control a commander, and yours is cast on turn nine on average — so budget three mana for each of them and stop planning free interaction you do not have.

VS STAX AND TAX. Flip to beatdown and race the lock's completion (strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial). Name the piece that beats you rather than the scariest permanent on the table: an untap denier, or anything taxing an activated ability, because your exit is an activated ability.

Eminence is why a tax rock does not beat you. It discounts every other Dragon spell from the command zone whether or not the commander is ever castable, so take the discount, cast the Dragon, and stop trying to cast him.

Bank the Treasure bursts and pay a whole tax in one lump — Goldspan Dragon, Old Gnawbone, Atsushi and Cavern-Hoard Dragon each convert one good combat into a turn's worth of mana. Point Generous Gift, Swords to Plowshares and Chaos Warp at whatever stops you untapping or attacking.

You need exactly one clean combat, because Ventmaw's loop funds itself from that point on (stack 003). Only three of your eleven interactive cards are counterspells and a counter answers a lock piece only on the way in, so keep a land untapped for the rest of them instead of jamming a fifth Dragon under the tax.

VS AGGRO. You are the control seat (strategy:whos-the-beatdown). Their maths is the worst at the table — roughly 120 combined life behind three defences (strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry) — and 20 of your creatures fly with toughness four or better, so a ground board never gets there. Block, eat the hits that do not matter, and let them keep swinging at whoever is racing them.

Develop on schedule anyway. Ramp or fixing is in hand by turn six in 71.6% of games, and holding it back to represent interaction you are not holding just loses the long game you were going to win.

Read Crux of Fate before you promise yourself it is one-sided. The non-Dragon mode kills Dragonspeaker Shaman and Rivaz of the Claw — your only two non-Dragon creatures, one of them a cost reducer and one of them a mana source. It is also {3}{B}{B} on 16 black sources, which lands on curve 44.6% of the time, so plan a line that wins without it.

Dragonback Assault costs you the same two bodies and nothing else: its three damage on entry kills no Dragon you own, because your lowest Dragon toughness is four. Fire it once Dragonspeaker Shaman has already bought you a discount. Blasphemous Act gets cheaper the wider they go, and with Wrathful Red Dragon out it stops being a reset and kills the aggro player outright (stack 004).

VS COMBO. Held answers rot, and the last profitable moment against a combo deck is their win attempt (strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy). Hold Counterspell, Swan Song, Dovin's Veto, Chaos Warp and Deflecting Swat for that turn and cast none of them earlier.

Race them rather than sitting in pure reaction. All three of your infinite lines need no mana beyond the pieces themselves, so take your own window (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window) — protection is in hand by turn six in 66.0% of games, which usually clears the bar for committing.

Save Teferi's Protection for exactly one of two turns: the turn their combo resolves, or the turn yours does. Do not spend it on a wrath you were going to rebuild from anyway.

VS GRAVEYARD DECKS AND GRAVEYARD HATE. These are two different problems and you should treat them that way.

Nothing in the deck touches an opposing graveyard, so a reanimator seat has to be beaten on the stack or on speed. Counter the enabler, not the body — once the fatty is on the battlefield you have no second answer to the yard that made it.

When the hate points at you, shrug and let it land. Patriarch's Bidding, Rivaz's once-a-turn cast from your yard and Haven of the Spirit Dragon's return are bonuses, not the spine, and a Bojuka Bog spent on you was not spent on the deck that needed it.

Hold your own Bidding for the token pods. Tokens never reach a graveyard as cards, so cast it after the table has been wiped and you get a fistful of Dragons back while they get almost nothing.
how_it_wins:
They count to nine in your command zone, see five colours, and file you under durdle. Let them keep that read — it is the only free thing you get all game. Eminence runs from the command zone, so every other Dragon spell you cast is {1} cheaper from your first upkeep, and nothing has to resolve for it to be true.

So stop building turns around the commander. He is cast on turn 8.967 on average, 0.0% of the time by turn six, and in 8,634 of 10,000 simulated games he never lands at all inside ten turns. Cast the discounted Dragon instead. Every time.

Your median kill is critical mass, and the order is the whole trick: payoff first, Dragon second. Dragon Tempest, Scourge of Valkas and Terror of the Peaks pay for every Dragon that enters after them and pay nothing for the ones already down. A payoff is in hand by turn six in 62.2% of games — so the turn one shows up early, play it into an empty board and be patient about it. Land Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm ahead of your top end; with Panharmonicon, Terror of the Peaks and Dragon Tempest already down, one Lathliss cast is 64 damage across twelve separately aimed instances (stack 002).

The unfair kill assembles in 3.6% of games by turn six. Aggravated Assault plus a mana dragon is your ceiling, not your schedule — take it when it arrives and never wait on it. When it does arrive, hold the enchantment until the turn it kills someone: all three of your infinites run through that one card, and Scourge of the Throne, the only other extra-combat effect in the 99, works once each turn and only when you attack the player at the highest life.

Count real mana before you swing. Haven of the Spirit Dragon, Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon, Unclaimed Territory, Rivaz of the Claw and an attacking Klauth all make spells-only mana, and an activated ability is not a spell — none of it pays Assault's {3}{R}{R}. Treasures do, so bank them: Old Gnawbone, Goldspan Dragon, Cavern-Hoard Dragon and a dead Atsushi all print mana nobody has restricted.

Early, you are the value seat, and you should enjoy it. Ramp, fix, let a louder player eat the removal, and keep one protection spell in hand — you have one by turn six in 66.0% of games, and that is the number that tells you when to commit the wave. Then take a single window. Hellkite Courser rents the commander out of the zone for one hasty attack, Sneak Attack drops Drakuseth for {R} (stack 005), Wrathful Red Dragon turns the next sweeper into a 39-point execution (stack 004). Take the turn that wins, not the turn that impresses.

combo_lines.001: The clause that decides this is one word inside Miirym's trigger: nontoken. Fifteen Faerie Dragons arrive on a single instruction and not one of them qualifies, so she copies nothing at all. Dragon Tempest carries no such reservation, and CR 603.2c splits one event with fifteen occurrences into fifteen separate triggers — each choosing its target as it goes on the stack (CR 115.1d), each recounting your Dragons at its own resolution (CR 608.2h). The holding: seventeen damage, fifteen times, with priority passing between every instalment. 255 available; the 30-life opponent is dead on the second trigger aimed at them, and anything still pointed at that player afterwards is countered on resolution (CR 608.2b).
combo_lines.002: Panharmonicon does not read the trigger. Its clause asks only what caused the trigger — an artifact or creature entering — so Miirym's 'nontoken Dragon' and Terror of the Peaks's 'another creature' are treated exactly alike, and each triggers an additional time (CR 603.2d). What keeps the cascade finite is the same word that bounded the last case: the copies are tokens, and every nontoken clause in the chain steps straight over them. The holding: one six-mana cast yields two nonlegendary Lathliss copies and 64 damage in twelve separately aimed instances — 36 from Terror, 28 from Tempest at optimal trigger ordering. Enough for the 32-life opponent. Not enough for both.
combo_lines.003: Savage Ventmaw's second sentence is an express override of the emptying rule. 'Until end of turn, you don't lose this mana as steps and phases end' displaces CR 106.4, so the attack mana walks out of combat and into your postcombat main phase intact. CR 107.4b closes the argument: a generic cost accepts mana of any type, so {G}{G}{G} pays Assault's {3}. The holding: one attack funds one extra combat and leaves {R} behind, which is a net gain of one mana per cycle rather than a break-even. The record is explicit that nothing in the rules bounds this loop. Blockers, removal and the sorcery-speed restriction bound it.
combo_lines.004: The doctrine on the record is CR 113.7a: once an ability has triggered it exists independently of its source, and destroying that source afterwards does not reach it. Three Dragons you control are dealt 13 in one event, so Wrathful Red Dragon triggers three times (CR 603.2c) — and the lethal-damage check (CR 704.5g) clears the battlefield before any target is chosen, which leaves players as the only legal targets that are not Dragons. Each dead Dragon still deals its 13, by last known information. The holding: 39 damage, all of it assignable to one opponent, and never enough for two. Two triggers is 26, which falls short.
combo_lines.005: Two zones settle this, and the record is unusually plain about it. Sneak Attack reaches 'a creature card from your hand'; a commander begins the game in the command zone (CR 903.6), and the command zone is not the hand. The claim that this line cheats The Ur-Dragon into play is refuted — from that zone the rules offer one route, the nine-mana cast plus tax (CR 903.8). Everything beneath the command zone is affirmed: Drakuseth enters for {R}, its ability fires because it was declared as an attacker rather than cast (CR 508.3a), haste permits the attack (CR 702.10b), and the 17 damage already dealt is a one-shot effect the mandatory sacrifice cannot undo (CR 610.1). Hellkite Courser is the card in this deck whose text names the command zone.
combo_lines.006: The point of law is a window most players never name. CR 118.2 grants you a chance to activate mana abilities while you are paying a cost, and a Treasure's tap-and-sacrifice is a mana ability that never uses the stack (CR 605.1a, CR 605.3b). Five Treasures therefore pay {3}{R}{R} in the middle of the activation with the lands untouched. Seven in per connection, five out per activation: the ledger runs +2 a cycle, and it sustains for as long as a creature deals five or more combat damage to a player each combat. The holding: this loop is bounded by the game, not by the mana — the win ends it mid-trigger (CR 104.2a), which is why the final count is 22 Treasures and not 29.

card_roles.The Ur-Dragon: Your discount engine, and it bills from the command zone — every other Dragon spell costs {1} less whether or not he ever touches the battlefield. Cast him only when nine mana is genuinely spare; the attack trigger that draws per attacking Dragon and drops a free permanent is a bonus you collect, never a turn you plan.
card_roles.Ancient Gold Dragon: One connection rolls a d20 and hands you that many flying bodies, which is your single biggest swing with Dragon Tempest already down (stack 001). Point it at the emptiest board at the table, not the scariest one.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Two-mana any-colour fixing in a five-colour deck. Play it on turn two ahead of almost anything else you could be doing.
card_roles.Blasphemous Act: It costs {1} less per creature on the battlefield, so by the time you want it the table has usually made it a one-mana reset. With Wrathful Red Dragon out it stops being a reset and becomes an execution (stack 004).
card_roles.Boros Charm: Four to the face, indestructible for everything you own, or double strike on one Dragon — pick the mode that ends the turn. The indestructible mode is your cheapest way through a sweeper, so hold it for that first.
card_roles.Breaching Dragonstorm: It digs to the first nonland card and casts it free at mana value 8 or less, which describes most of your top end. Fire it on a turn you need a body immediately, not on a turn you want value.
card_roles.Cavern-Hoard Dragon: It costs {X} less for the artifacts an opponent controls, so it lands early against Treasure and equipment seats and mints Treasures back on every hit. Its pairing with Aggravated Assault still needs a stack scenario — take the body and the mana, not the promise.
card_roles.Chaos Warp: Your only clean answer to a resolved artifact or enchantment, and it hits any permanent at all. Aim it at whatever stops your combats, and accept that they reveal the top of their library and may keep a permanent off it.
card_roles.Chromatic Lantern: It turns every land you control into an any-colour source, which is worth far more than the one mana it makes itself. Play it the turn before you need a double-pip spell, never on the turn you already need it.
card_roles.Counterspell: Two mana to say no. Hold it for somebody's win attempt, not for the first scary creature you happen to see.
card_roles.Crux of Fate: Choose destroy all non-Dragon creatures and it is a one-sided wipe that leaves your board standing. The cost is Dragonspeaker Shaman and Rivaz of the Claw, who are the two creatures here that are not Dragons — count them before you cast it.
card_roles.Dovin's Veto: It counters the noncreature spell and cannot be countered itself. Save it for the combo piece or the sweeper, the two things that actually beat you.
card_roles.Dracogenesis: Every Dragon spell you cast is free while this is on the battlefield. Land it and empty your hand the same turn, because nobody is going to let you untap with it.
card_roles.Dragon Tempest: Two mana, and every Dragon entering afterwards throws damage equal to your Dragon count. Get it down before the Dragons — it pays nothing at all for what has already landed.
card_roles.Dragon's Hoard: Any-colour fixing that grows a gold counter per Dragon entering, and each counter cashes for a card. Play it early enough that the counters have time to stack up; it is real card advantage the role taxonomy does not credit.
card_roles.Dragonback Assault: Three damage on entry clears a small board, and afterwards every land drop is a 4/4 flier. It is your best single answer to a token pod — and it kills Dragonspeaker Shaman and Rivaz of the Claw, so sequence around them.
card_roles.Dragonlord Dromoka: Cannot be countered and shuts your opponents out of your turn entirely — this is the body you cast into open blue mana. It also makes your alpha strike safe from instant-speed tricks.
card_roles.Dragonlord Kolaghan: Haste for the whole team, which turns every fresh Dragon into damage the turn it lands. Treat the 10-life punisher clause as a coincidence you occasionally profit from, never a plan.
card_roles.Dragonspeaker Shaman: {2} off every Dragon spell for three mana, and the best turn-three play in the deck. Keep opening hands that contain it — a reducer only shows up by turn six 33.2% of the time.
card_roles.Drakuseth, Maw of Flames: Ten damage split across three targets every single time it attacks, before blockers matter at all. Cheat it in with Sneak Attack on the turn you need that damage right now (stack 005).
card_roles.Eerie Interlude: Blink your team out of a sweeper and they come back at end of turn, re-firing every enters trigger on the way in. Hold it as protection first and value second.
card_roles.Encroaching Dragonstorm: Two basics on arrival, and it bounces itself when a Dragon enters, so it is ramp you get to replay. Cast it on four when nothing better exists and re-buy it forever.
card_roles.Enlightened Tutor: One mana finds Aggravated Assault, Panharmonicon or whichever protection artifact you are missing. Cast it the turn before you need the card, never on the turn you do — it goes on top of your library, not into your hand.
card_roles.Farseek: It fetches any nonbasic with a basic land type, which covers the shocks and the Triomes in this list. Two mana that ramps and fixes at once, and you should almost always take the dual.
card_roles.Flawless Maneuver: Free while you control a commander, and your whole team becomes indestructible. Never let it rot in hand while you decline to commit the board — and price it at three mana in the games where the commander never lands.
card_roles.Garruk's Uprising: Trample for the team and a card every time a 4-power creature enters, which is nearly every creature you play. This is the draw engine the audit says you are six cards short of.
card_roles.Generous Gift: Three mana destroys any permanent and hands back a 3/3. Spend it on the thing that beats you, not on the biggest body at the table.
card_roles.Goldspan Dragon: A hasty 5-power flier that mints a Treasure whenever it attacks or gets targeted, and its Treasures make two mana each. That is unrestricted mana, so it is one of the few things here that can legally pay Aggravated Assault.
card_roles.Hellkite Courser: This is the card that genuinely pulls The Ur-Dragon out of the command zone — hasty, for one attack, with the eminence draw trigger live and no tax added (stack 005). Attack with everything the turn it enters.
card_roles.Herald's Horn: {1} off every Dragon creature spell plus a free look at the top of your library each upkeep. Name Dragon and never think about it again.
card_roles.Heroic Intervention: Two mana buys hexproof and indestructible for every permanent you own. Hold it for the turn you commit the wave, which is the turn it is worth a card.
card_roles.Klauth, Unrivaled Ancient: Attacking adds mana equal to your attackers' total power, which is an enormous number and strictly for casting spells. Spend it on a second Dragon postcombat; it can never pay an activated ability, so it cannot fund Aggravated Assault.
card_roles.Lathliss, Dragon Queen: Every nontoken Dragon after her drags a 5/5 along, and her {1}{R} pump turns a stalled board into lethal. With Miirym, Panharmonicon, Terror of the Peaks and Dragon Tempest down, one cast of her is 64 damage (stack 002).
card_roles.Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm: She copies every nontoken Dragon you land after her, from behind ward {2}. Sequence her ahead of your top end and expect the table to answer her first — she is the scariest fair card you own.
card_roles.Mox Jasper: Free any-colour mana the moment you control a Dragon. Keep a Dragon on the battlefield and this is a land you never had to draw.
card_roles.Nature's Lore: Two mana for any Forest card, and it arrives untapped — your Forest-typed duals included. Take the dual over the basic unless you genuinely need green tomorrow.
card_roles.Old Gnawbone: Every point of combat damage your team deals comes back as Treasure, and Treasure is the one mana here that can pay Aggravated Assault. With Assault down, one unblocked connection ends the whole table in sequence (stack 006).
card_roles.Panharmonicon: It doubles every trigger caused by a creature entering — Miirym, Lathliss, Terror, Tempest, all of it (stack 002). Play it before the wave, never after it.
card_roles.Patriarch's Bidding: Name Dragon and everything you have lost comes back at once, including whatever a sweeper just ate. Save it for after the wrath, and remember every other player names something too.
card_roles.Relic of Legends: Any-colour mana, and it taps your untapped legendary creatures for more of it. In a list carrying 14 legendary permanents that is a Signet that grows all game.
card_roles.Return of the Wildspeaker: Draw cards equal to your biggest non-Human's power — usually five or seven here — or pump the team for the kill. It is an instant, so cast it after blockers are declared and let them choose wrong.
card_roles.Rishkar's Expertise: A giant refill off your largest body plus a free spell at mana value 5 or less. Cast it with Terror of the Peaks or Scourge of Valkas still in hand and take both halves.
card_roles.Rivaz of the Claw: Two mana in any colours toward Dragon creature spells, plus one Dragon recast from your graveyard each turn. Note what he is not: a 3/3 Lizard Warlock, so your own Dragonback Assault and Crux of Fate's non-Dragon mode both kill him, and his mana is spells-only and will never pay Aggravated Assault.
card_roles.Roiling Dragonstorm: Two mana to draw two and discard one, and it returns to your hand whenever a Dragon enters. Replay it every turn you have two mana lying idle.
card_roles.Sarkhan's Triumph: Instant-speed tutor for any Dragon in the deck — engine piece or answer body, your choice. Cast it at the end of the turn before your big one.
card_roles.Savage Ventmaw: Attacking adds {R}{R}{R}{G}{G}{G} that survives the phase change, which is a whole extra Dragon in your postcombat main. With Aggravated Assault it pays for its own extra combat and leaves {R} behind (stack 003).
card_roles.Scourge of Valkas: Damage equal to your Dragon count every time a Dragon enters, itself included. It is Dragon Tempest on a 4/4 flier, so land it before the flood rather than during it.
card_roles.Scourge of the Throne: Attack the player at the highest life and you untap all attackers for a free extra combat, once each turn. It is the only extra-combat effect in the 99 besides Aggravated Assault, so point the first attack at the table leader deliberately.
card_roles.Skyshroud Claim: Two Forest cards onto the battlefield untapped on turn four, and your Forest-typed duals qualify. It fixes while it ramps, which is the only thing turn four is for here.
card_roles.Sol Ring: Two colourless on turn one or two. Always keep it, always resolve it first.
card_roles.Swan Song: One mana answers the sweeper, the ritual or the enchantment; they get a 2/2 flier and you keep your board. Take that trade every time it is offered.
card_roles.Swords to Plowshares: One mana exiles anything, which is the cleanest answer in the 99. Spend it on the creature that beats you, not on the first one you meet.
card_roles.Teferi's Protection: Your board phases out and your life cannot change until your next turn. Hold it for the sweeper or the lethal swing — it is the best card you can have in hand on your big turn.
card_roles.Temur Ascendancy: Haste for everything and a card whenever a 4-power creature enters, which here means nearly every Dragon. Every body you cast attacks the same turn it lands.
card_roles.Terror of the Peaks: Every creature entering afterwards throws its own power at any target, and opponents pay three life just to aim a spell at it. Land it first, then flood the board.
card_roles.Thrakkus the Butcher: Attacking doubles the power of every Dragon you control, which is the fastest route from a fair board to a lethal one. Count the damage before you declare attackers; it usually kills somebody you did not expect.
card_roles.Tiamat: Casting it fetches five differently named Dragons straight to hand — take the engine pieces, not the biggest bodies. Eminence and the reducers make the seven-drop honest, and it is the one God card The World Tree can find.
card_roles.Urza's Incubator: {2} off every Dragon creature spell for three mana. Alongside Dragonspeaker Shaman it turns your entire top end into midrange.
card_roles.Utvara Hellkite: Every attacking Dragon brings a 6/6 flier with it, so one combat under this ends most boards. Keep it alive through a single turn cycle and the long game is already yours.
card_roles.Worldly Tutor: One mana at instant speed for any creature in the deck. Fetch the piece the turn before you need it, not the turn you are already dead.
card_roles.Aggravated Assault: The win condition and the loudest tell in one card: {3}{R}{R} untaps your team and buys another combat, and all three infinites in the 99 run through it. Hold it for the turn it kills somebody, and remember your Dragon-restricted mana cannot pay the activation.
card_roles.Korlessa, Scale Singer: Two mana lets you cast Dragons straight off the top of your library, with the top card always visible. She is a 1/4 Dragon, so your own Dragonback Assault does not touch her and Crux of Fate's non-Dragon mode leaves her standing — deploy her early and leave her there.
card_roles.Deflecting Swat: Free while you control a commander, and it re-aims any spell or ability — the removal pointed at Aggravated Assault, or somebody else's tutor. Keep a red source up on the turns that matter, because the commander is usually not on the battlefield to make it free.
card_roles.Wrathful Red Dragon: Damage dealt to your Dragons gets thrown at any non-Dragon target, so a sweeper becomes an execution: three Dragons dealt 13 is 39 at one opponent (stack 004). Get it down early and let them cast the wrath.
card_roles.Sneak Attack: One red mana puts any Dragon from your hand onto the battlefield with haste, and every attack and enters trigger fires before the end-step sacrifice (stack 005). It reaches your hand only — never plan on it for the commander.
card_roles.Atsushi, the Blazing Sky: A four-mana flier that pays you when it dies: two cards to play, or three Treasures that pay for anything, including Aggravated Assault. Block with it happily.
card_roles.Blood Crypt: Pay the 2 life and take it untapped. Black is your scarcest colour on curve at 26.1%, so the tempo beats the life almost every time.
card_roles.Breeding Pool: Your untapped green-blue source for Korlessa on turn two or Miirym on curve. The 2 life is cheap on the turns those matter.
card_roles.Canopy Vista: Green and white, untapped once two basics are down. Lead with basics early and this stops costing you a turn.
card_roles.Cinder Glade: Red and green untapped once you control two basics — the two colours this deck leans on hardest. Sequence a basic first and it is a dual.
card_roles.City of Brass: Any colour, untapped, for one damage a tap. In a five-colour deck that is the cheapest fixing you will ever buy; pay it and stop thinking about it.
card_roles.Clifftop Retreat: Red and white untapped as long as a Mountain or Plains is already down. Sequence your basics so that it is.
card_roles.Command Tower: Any of your five colours, untapped, for nothing at all. Play it the moment you draw it.
card_roles.Exotic Orchard: It reads your opponents' lands, so it is a second Command Tower at a multicolour table and much less at a mono-colour one. Check the board before you build a turn on it.
card_roles.Fabled Passage: Fetch a basic, and it untaps once four lands are down. Go get the colour you are actually missing — usually the Swamp or the Island — not the one you already have three of.
card_roles.Forbidden Orchard: Any colour untapped, and each tap hands an opponent a 1/1. Tap it when the mana matters more than the chump blocker you are donating.
card_roles.Forest: Green for Nature's Lore, Farseek and the green half of Savage Ventmaw. Green is your most reliable colour at 84.9% on curve precisely because of these.
card_roles.Glacial Fortress: White and blue untapped if a Plains or Island is already down — your two thinnest colours, so drop it on a turn you can afford to have it tapped.
card_roles.Haven of the Spirit Dragon: Colourless, or any colour that may only cast a Dragon creature spell, plus a late buy-back for a dead Dragon. Never count its coloured mana toward an activated ability.
card_roles.Island: Your only blue basic, and therefore the Counterspell and Korlessa source. Fetch it with Fabled Passage when you are holding either.
card_roles.Jetmir's Garden: Three colours on a tapped land, or a {3} cycle when you are flooded out. Play it on a turn you were never going to spend everything anyway.
card_roles.Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon: Colourless, or Dragon-spell-only colour, and it sacrifices itself later to find a Dragon. Like Haven, its coloured mana casts and never activates.
card_roles.Mountain: Your most-demanded colour on a land that always comes in untapped — red is 46.5% of your pips. Fetch these first when a triple-red spell is in hand.
card_roles.Overgrown Tomb: Black and green untapped for 2 life. Black sources are scarce enough here that you should almost always pay it.
card_roles.Path of Ancestry: It enters tapped, but every creature it casts that shares a type with your commander scries, and nearly every creature you play does. Drop it on a turn you were not spending all your mana.
card_roles.Reflecting Pool: It copies whatever your other lands can make, so it is superb late and close to blank on turn one. Hold it behind a real dual whenever you can.
card_roles.Rootbound Crag: Red and green untapped once a Mountain or Forest is down. Sequence basics first and it never costs you tempo.
card_roles.Savage Lands: Three colours, always tapped — one of only five lands here that give you no choice about it. Play it on a turn where a tapped land costs you nothing.
card_roles.Steam Vents: Blue and red for 2 life. Take it untapped whenever you want Counterspell live inside this turn cycle.
card_roles.Stomping Ground: Red and green for 2 life — the two colours your curve leans on hardest, so pay it more often than you don't.
card_roles.Sulfur Falls: Blue and red untapped once an Island or Mountain is down. It is your smoothest way to hold up a counter and still cast a Dragon.
card_roles.Swamp: Your single black basic, and the fetch target that turns on Patriarch's Bidding or Crux of Fate. Go get it the moment either is in hand.
card_roles.The World Tree: Green while it stands alone, and all-colour fixing for every land you control once six are down. Its ten-mana ability puts Tiamat onto the battlefield — she is the only God card in the 99, so it finds exactly one thing.
card_roles.Unclaimed Territory: Name Dragon and it makes any colour for your creature spells. That mana casts; it never activates.
card_roles.Ziatora's Proving Ground: Black, red and green on a tapped land, or a {3} cycle when your lands are already plentiful. Take the fixing early and the cycle late.

mulligan:
Keeping a seven means two to four lands and one piece of acceleration. Two lands and a seven-drop is not a keep, however good the seven-drop looks.

The acceleration that decides games is a cost reducer. Ramp or fixing shows up by turn six in 71.6% of games; a reducer in only 33.2%. So when Dragonspeaker Shaman, Urza's Incubator or Herald's Horn is already sitting in your opener, stop reading the hand and keep it. Reducer plus ramp together — the hand that casts a turn-five Dragon nobody expected — arrives by turn six 23.1% of the time. Never ship one of those hunting for prettier Dragons.

The second thing to want is a payoff before your first big body: Dragon Tempest, Garruk's Uprising, Roiling Dragonstorm, Korlessa. One is drawn by turn six 62.2% of the time. Having it on turn two is how you beat that number instead of matching it.

Never mulligan toward the commander. Eminence works from the command zone, so a hand that can eventually cast him is worth nothing over a hand that never will.

Ship two shapes on sight. Lands plus top end with nothing to do on turn three — your land drops fall to 60.3% on turn five and 49.7% on turn six, so the bridge is not coming to you. And hands whose colours cannot cast their own cards: black is the one that fails, at 11 land sources and a 26.1% on-curve rate, and remember that Haven, Maelstrom, Unclaimed Territory, Rivaz and Klauth only ever pay for spells.

Aggravated Assault in an opener is a hold, not a reason to keep. It needs a body, funding and a turn where it kills somebody, and on turn three it only announces you. Protection is a genuine keep-bonus — Teferi's Protection, Heroic Intervention, Flawless Maneuver — because holding one is what lets you commit the board later.

Trust your sevens. The simulator keeps 75.1% of first hands at 0.313 mean mulligans, which means the hand in front of you is usually the hand. Mulligan for function, never for glamour.
upgrades:
Ten names, and eight of them open a combo line the record has not settled — every one of those eight reads 'needs a stack scenario'. Six pair with Aggravated Assault, which is a comment on the deck rather than on the list: one enchantment carries all three contained infinites, so a single Naturalize is worth three kill lines here, and a second card name for that architecture is the cheapest thing anybody could buy.

The two that route around it are the interesting ones. Hellkite Charger puts the extra combat on a Dragon body, so the eminence discount and all five Dragon-restricted mana sources reach the cast even though the {5}{R}{R} activation still needs unrestricted mana. Helm of the Host pairs with Scourge of the Throne, already in the 99 — the only line on the list that touches Aggravated Assault nowhere at all, and at 6,177 decks the least-played of the eight.

Popularity is a headcount, not evidence, and it spreads wide. The Reaver Cleaver plus Assault sits at 34,407 decks, the most-played line any candidate opens, and it costs three mana to put 'create that many Treasure tokens' onto an equipment instead of onto one specific seven-drop. Sword of Feast and Famine is 28,954 and Ancient Copper Dragon 22,541, down to Helm's 6,177. Those numbers count how many people believe a line. The verified stamps sit only on the engines already sleeved.

Two figures point somewhere other than combat. Three Visits is EDHREC rank 42, by a distance the most-played card on the list, and the obsolescence index traces it to Skyshroud Claim at 0.9936 similarity for two less mana value. Read the rest of that entry, though: Nature's Lore at 0.9944 and Farseek at 0.9902 obsolete the same card and both are already in the 99, so this is copy three of an effect the deck has twice decided it trusts. And card advantage is the deepest hole on the audit at 4 against a target of 10, which is the whole reason an eight-mana Dragon that draws a d20 of cards makes a list otherwise entirely about combat.

One caveat, sized honestly. No pick on the list moves the computed floor off 4. The bracket is already paid for by three two-card infinites that each assemble at zero extra mana, so nothing here is a power purchase — it is redundancy for a plan that currently rests on one card.
mana_base:
Thirty-four land copies across 29 entries, against the 36 to 38 the template asks for. Sixteen of those 34 have the words 'enters tapped' printed somewhere on them, which reads as 47% and a disaster — but only five enter tapped unconditionally, and five against a ceiling of eight is the number the audit actually scores. The tapland axis passes comfortably. The land count is the one that misses.

Watch where that bill lands. 3.042 mana on turn three, 4.937 on turn six, 6.539 on turn ten, with the land drop holding at 88.3% on turn three and then falling through 60.3% and 49.7% on exactly the turns a deck with 28 five-plus-drops has to start deploying. This base rarely misses a colour. It misses turns.

Pip share and source share disagree hardest on red. Red is 46.5% of the pip load carried by 28.6% of the sources — 47 pips across 32 cards, as many as three in a single cost. Green is nearly square at 21.8% of pips on 25.7% of sources, and it is the colour whose lands keep pace: 84.9% on curve from lands alone, against red's 58.0%, because green asks one pip at a time where red's effective ask is two. Black runs the disagreement backwards, 7.9% of pips on 15.7% of sources, and still finishes worst on curve at 26.1% — a six-card splash sitting on 11 land sources.

Six rocks and three dorks are what close the gaps, and they close them unevenly: black to 44.6%, red to 76.4%, white to 78.7%, blue to 81.0%, green to 92.7%. Five of the nine make any colour at all — Arcane Signet, Chromatic Lantern, Dragon's Hoard, Mox Jasper, Relic of Legends. That is why the source budget passes at 46 against a floor of 45 while the land count fails: the fixing package is doing the colour work and the lands are only doing the mana.

Then the 90% yardstick, which is worth reading correctly. It wants 36 black and 36 red sources inside a 34-land deck — a measuring stick, not a possibility, and it reads that way in every five-colour list ever built. Two things it refuses to count. Five sources make spells-only mana, which is real for casting and worth exactly nothing to an activated ability. And Treasures out of Old Gnawbone, Goldspan Dragon, Atsushi and Cavern-Hoard Dragon are unrestricted income nobody can forecast by looking at your lands.
